content: Algorithm complexity measures how computational resources (time and space) scale with input size, providing a framework for comparing algorithm efficiency. Big O notation expresses the upper bound of an algorithm's growth rate, ignoring coefficients and lower-order terms to focus on asymptotic behavior. Common time complexities include: O(1) - constant time (like array index access), O(log n) - logarithmic time (like binary search), O(n) - linear time (like linear search), O(n log n) - linearithmic time (like efficient sorting algorithms), O(nÂ²) - quadratic time (like simple sorting algorithms), and O(2â¿) - exponential time (like brute force solutions). In searching algorithms, linear search checks each element sequentially, requiring O(n) time in the worst case. Binary search divides a sorted collection in half repeatedly, achieving O(log n) time but requiring pre-sorted data. Hashing can achieve average-case O(1) search time but may degrade to O(n) in worst cases with many collisions. Space complexity similarly describes memory usage growth. Some algorithms trade increased space usage for faster runtime (space-time tradeoff). Understanding complexity helps programmers predict how algorithms will perform with large datasets and choose appropriate approaches for specific problems. While Big O provides theoretical scaling behavior, practical performance also depends on implementation details, hardware, and constant factors that become significant with smaller inputs.

scenario.title: Search Strategy Challenge
scenario.content: Students participate in a virtual scavenger hunt where they design and implement different search algorithms to find hidden items across a school campus. The simulation visualizes algorithm execution in real-time, showing how different approaches navigate the search space. Students can implement and compare linear search, binary search, depth-first search, breadth-first search, hashing, and other strategies across various scenarios. The system tracks and graphs key metrics including time complexity, space usage, and actual runtime as input size increases. Interactive elements allow students to modify search spaces, add obstacles or shortcuts, and introduce randomization to test algorithm robustness. Challenge modes require students to select or design optimal algorithms for specific constraints, such as limited memory, distributed search teams, or partially reliable information.

hypothesis.description: Students will compare algorithm efficiency by analyzing how different search strategies scale with input size. They will predict performance characteristics using Big O notation, and select appropriate algorithms based on problem constraints and performance requirements.
